## Incident Report — PCAP Forensic Analysis
**Evidence:** `2022-01-07-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (5,880 frames, ~4.6 MB, capture window 2022-01-07 20:04:09–20:16:40 local). No separate IDS/Suricata alert files were present in the evidence directory; findings below are derived entirely from the packet capture using tshark.

### 1. Infected / victim host
| Attribute | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 192.168.1.216 | DHCP, all sessions |
| MAC | 9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9 | ARP, DHCP |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-GXMYNO2** | DHCP Option 12 (client hostname) and Kerberos client principal `DESKTOP-GXMYNO2$` both agree on this spelling. Note: NetBIOS Name Service broadcasts from this same IP/MAC consistently show a one-letter variant, `DESKTOP-GXNYNO2` — flagging the discrepancy since it appears in the raw traffic, but treating DHCP+Kerberos (two independent, authoritative protocols) as canonical. |
| Logged-in domain user | **steve.smith** (domain SPOONWATCH / SPOONWATCH.NET) | Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ CNameString and SMB2/NTLM session auth both show `steve.smith`, domain `SPOONWATCH` |
| Domain controller | SPOONWATCH-DC, 192.168.1.2 | DNS, NBNS, Kerberos, LDAP/CLDAP |

The host performed normal domain logon (Kerberos/LDAP/CLDAP to the DC) and routine Windows Update / Microsoft telemetry traffic; that traffic is benign and excluded from the IOC list below.

### 2. Malware family
**Vidar Stealer** (information-stealing malware / loader). **Attribution is behavioral, not signature-confirmed** — no IDS/Suricata alert artifacts were supplied with this evidence, so this call rests entirely on matching the C2 protocol and file-naming conventions observed in the capture, not on a rule hit.

Behavioral evidence for Vidar:
- The infected host issues seven sequential HTTP POSTs to a `/osk/` path on the C2, each named `N.jpg` (`1.jpg`–`7.jpg`), with a 25-byte multipart-form checkin body and no browser User-Agent header, `Accept-Language: ru-RU,ru;q=0.9,en;q=0.8` hardcoded.
- Every one of the seven "images" returned (`Content-Type: image/jpeg`) is actually a **Windows PE32 DLL**, not a JPEG. Their embedded strings identify the classic Vidar dependency bundle used to read Firefox/Chrome SQLite profile stores: `sqlite3.dll`, `nss3.dll`/`freebl3.dll`, `softokn3.dll`/`nssdbm3.dll`, `msvcp140.dll`/`vcruntime140.dll`.
- After the module downloads, the host POSTs an empty checkin to `/osk//main.php`, then uploads a ZIP archive (`_586169512120.zip`) to `/osk/` via `multipart/form-data`. Extracted, the archive contains the exact Vidar exfiltration folder layout: `autofill/`, `cc/` (credit cards), `cookies/`, plus `passwords.txt`, `system.txt`, `outlook.txt` — each per-browser file named `<Browser Name>_<Profile>.txt` (e.g. `Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`), which is Vidar's signature stealer-log naming scheme. Most fields are empty in this run except `cookies/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt` (126,739 bytes of actual stolen cookie data).
- The C2 server banner (`Apache/2.4.12 (Win32) OpenSSL/1.0.1m PHP/5.3.29 mod_wsgi/4.4.11 Python/2.7.10`) is consistent with the low-cost, Windows-hosted PHP panels commonly used by Vidar operators.

No initial-access artifact (phishing document, dropper download) is present in this capture — the earliest ~200 seconds contain only DHCP/AD/Kerberos and Windows Update traffic before the C2 beaconing begins at t+202s, meaning the stealer was already executing on the host when the capture started (or delivery occurred out-of-band before capture).

### 3. Indicators of compromise (all observed directly in traffic)

**Command-and-control**
- `2.56.57.108:80` — sole external C2 endpoint; contacted by hardcoded IP literal (no DNS resolution observed, no malicious domain present in this capture — all DNS activity is legitimate Microsoft/AD traffic)

**Malicious URLs**
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//1.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//2.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//3.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//4.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//5.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//6.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//7.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//main.php`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk/` (used for the exfil upload)

**Transferred files (downloaded modules, disguised as JPEGs, all PE32 DLLs)**

| Delivered as | Size (bytes) | SHA256 |
|---|---|---|
| 1.jpg | 645,592 | `16574f51785b0e2fc29c2c61477eb47bb39f714829999511dc8952b43ab17660` |
| 2.jpg | 334,288 | `a770ecba3b08bbabd0a567fc978e50615f8b346709f8eb3cfacf3faab24090ba` |
| 3.jpg | 137,168 | `3fe6b1c54b8cf28f571e0c5d6636b4069a8ab00b4f11dd842cfec00691d0c9cd` |
| 4.jpg | 440,120 | `334e69ac9367f708ce601a6f490ff227d6c20636da5222f148b25831d22e13d4` |
| 5.jpg | 1,246,160 | `e2935b5b28550d47dc971f456d6961f20d1633b4892998750140e0eaa9ae9d78` |
| 6.jpg | 144,848 | `43536adef2ddcc811c28d35fa6ce3031029a2424ad393989db36169ff2995083` |
| 7.jpg | 83,784 | `c40bb03199a2054dabfc7a8e01d6098e91de7193619effbd0f142a7bf031c14d` |

**Transferred file (exfiltrated data, uploaded by victim to C2)**
- Filename: `_586169512120.zip`
- Multipart upload size: 379,629 bytes; extracted ZIP payload: 379,485 bytes
- SHA256 (extracted ZIP content): `618cbd9e2554807aaa9a584219f261fbc835723664ad6f0130f0b141cfd75ffb`
- Contents: `autofill/`, `cc/`, `cookies/` (per-browser: Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge), `passwords.txt`, `system.txt`, `outlook.txt`

### 4. Bottom line
DESKTOP-GXMYNO2 (192.168.1.216, MAC 9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9), logged in as domain user `steve.smith` on SPOONWATCH.NET, is actively communicating with a Vidar Stealer C2 at 2.56.57.108:80 (behavioral attribution — no signature evidence supplied). It downloaded seven DLL components disguised as JPEGs and exfiltrated a ZIP archive of browser autofill/credit-card/cookie data back to the same server. Recommend isolating the host, resetting `steve.smith`'s domain credentials, and blocking 2.56.57.108 at the perimeter.
